results.title: Preparing your replication package for Papers and Proceedings - Office of the AEA Data Editor
results.content: The AEA Data Editor’s mission is to design and oversee the AEA journals’ strategy for archiving and curating research data and promoting reproducible research. Much of the preparation for the replication packages for papers published in Papers and Proceedings is the same as for the AEA journals, see Step 1 and Step 2. Your replication package must nevertheless be fully compliant with the AEA Data and Code Availability Policy. Should a reader or user of your replication package find errors or omissions at a later stage, you will be asked to remedy the situation in line with our Policy on Revisions of Data and Code Deposits. > The use of the AEA Data and Code Repository is strongly encouraged. Suggested: The abstract from the article and/or a note that this is data and/or code accompanying the article. The README content must contain all the required elements as per the AEA Data and Code Availability Policy.

results.title: Create a Codebook
results.content: # Create a Codebook. A codebook is an essential document that informs the data user about the study, data file(s), variables, categories, etc., that make up a complete dataset. To create a codebook, information about the study, files, and variables must be known. (See the DDI Glossary for more information about study-level and variable-level metadata.) Information can sometimes be provided by a researcher in a readme file (e.g., a text file), or be embedded in a datafile package (e.g., SPSS allows for column names / labels / missing values / notes), and so on. **Tip:** *Don’t worry if you don’t currently have any DDI or structured metadata to work with, as there are a number of tools that you can use to extract file- and variable-level metadata (such as the variable names, labels, categories, values, frequency counts, etc.) found in your completed dataset.*. There are a number of tools that can create DDI for the creation of a structured codebook.

results.title: Documentation & Metadata - Research Data Management - Research Guides at University of Winnipeg
results.content:
Title: Documentation & Metadata - Research Data Management - Research Guides at University of Winnipeg
# Research Data Management. ## Research Data Management Librarian. Documentation is an important part of data management. Your data is only useful to yourself and others if you have adequately described your dataset and documented your processes. This includes describing when, why and how the data was collected or generated, what the variables mean, how it was analyzed and how the final dataset was created. Good documentation starts with good file management practices, including file naming conventions. The earlier a file naming convention is established in a research project, the better. * [File Naming Conventions [Harvard]](https://datamanagement.hms.harvard.edu/plan-design/file-naming-conventions). * [Organising & Example Folder Structure [UK Data Service]](https://ukdataservice.ac.uk/learning-hub/research-data-management/format-your-data/organising/). Guide for how best to keep track of your data files. * [Organize [UBC Library]](https://researchdata.library.ubc.ca/plan/organize-your-data/). ## ReadMe Files. A readme file provides information about a dataset and is intended to help ensure that the data can be correctly interpreted, by yourself at a later date or by others when sharing or publishing data. * [README File Generator [FRDR]](https://frdr-readme-generator.vercel.app/). This README file generator is maintained by the Federated Research Data Repository (https://www.frdr-dfdr.ca/). This tool allows researchers and data depositors to identify and populate relevant information to describe and contextualize datasets. Exported as plain text (.txt), the README file is suitable to document data for FRDR or other repositories. Created by Cornell University's Research Data Management Service Group. * [Writing README style metadata [Cornell]](https://data.research.cornell.edu/content/readme). Created by Cornell University's Research Data Management Service Group. * [Creating a README for your dataset [UBC]](https://osf.io/aqxw3/). ## Codebooks and Data Dictionaries. Codebooks and data dictionaries are two forms of structured documentation used to d*efine variables*. A codebook is a document commonly included with datasets in the social and behavioral sciences intended to assist with understanding the contents and structure of those datasets. A typical data dictionary might contain columns for variable name (exactly as it appears in the dataset), a more descriptive human-readable variable name, unit of measurement, allowed values, a definition of the variable, and additional explanation, comments, or notes for each variable. * [How to Make a Data Dictionary [OSF]](https://help.osf.io/article/217-how-to-make-a-data-dictionary). * [Creating a Codebook in SPSS [Kent State]](https://libguides.library.kent.edu/SPSS/Codebooks). This tool helps you create a codebook for your data tables with ease. * << **Previous:** Data Management Plans (DMPs).
